items.title: Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: And that’s what Alfred Lion used for rehearsing bands before taking them to Rudy Van Gelder’s.

ctx.x: I’ll say this, at one point my knees were shaking you know. You know when I decided to leave Howard University with my pharmacy studies and grapple with this thing, that was the moment where I said I know I can do this. And so anything that came after that was like gravy for me because I, you know, I knew I could play that trumpet now the way I was hearing it. And so what stood out for me was that Jackie McLean, so I was sent to Jackie McLean, who actually is the guy responsible for me being where I am in terms…

And he says, “Do you have any tunes?” I said, “Yes I do.” He says, “Let me hear them, let me play them.” He says, “Okay I’m putting you on my next record date.” Now I’ve told that story many times and every time people said you’ve got to be kidding. He hadn’t heard you yet. I said, “Well he was going on what Jim Harrison said, ‘Hey you know there’s a new trumpet player in town.’” You know. Boom. And so, and then to get on that, there was a place called Len Oliver’s Studio, it was a famous place on 89th and…
That’s a terrific story. I’m going to make a proposal here. We’ve been talking for an hour and I wonder if I could engage you for a part 2 in the near future?

items.title: Charles Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: But the secret of Rudy Van Gelder was his microphones.

ctx.x: Yeah, there wasn’t a practice of wearing earphones. I mean I suppose they were in use but I don’t recall any use of headphones. They were all in a sort of semi horseshoe set up, the piano the farthest away, and then bass and drums right together, no partitions or anything. And the horns facing the piano. So it was sort of like a little J type of thing. But the secret of Rudy Van Gelder was his microphones.
